abstract:
Genomics relies on both short-read and long-read sequencing, and keeping both is essential.

The post Why Genomics Won’t Converge on One Technology appeared first on GEN - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News.

metadata.author: Corinna Singleman, PhD

content.value:
For the past two years, I have been asking people at genomics conferences a simple question: Why is short-read sequencing so much less expensive than long-read sequencing?

These are people who use sequencing technologies every day. Most don’t have an answer. Those who do usually point to scale or maturity. Short-read sequencing has been around longer, the argument goes, so of course it costs less.

But that explanation assumes that with sufficient time and investment, long-read sequencing should catch up on cost. I don’t think that necessarily follows. To understand why, we need to look at what each technology is actually measuring.

Start with the measurement

Short-read sequencing makes a difficult measurement easier by making many copies of the same DNA fragment and reading them together. Rather than detecting a signal from one molecule, it measures the combined signal from thousands. This is ensemble detection. Individual molecules can behave imperfectly while the group still produces a usable answer.

Why not do the same thing with longer fragments? Because the molecules have to stay synchronized. At each sequencing cycle, they need to be reading the same position. Some fall behind while others move ahead. Those differences accumulate.

Consider a simplified example in which each cycle keeps 99.9% of molecules in phase. After 150 cycles, about 86% remain synchronized. After 10,000 cycles, only about 0.004% do. The same chemistry that produces a strong signal over a short read produces essentially no synchronized signal over a long one.

Long-read sequencing gets around this problem by measuring individual molecules. It no longer needs a population of molecules to stay in step. But it also loses the stronger signal that ensemble detection provides. Detecting individual molecular events requires greater sensitivity and imposes different constraints on chemistry and measurement time.

That is a different engineering problem, not simply an earlier stage of the same one. It is why I expect short-read sequencing to retain a cost advantage even as long-read technologies improve. That is not a reason to dismiss long reads, but it is a reason to distinguish questions that require long-range sequence from those that require long-range structure.

Ask what information is needed

The next question is whether we need to sequence every base to get the information we’re after. Often, we don’t. Structural variants, copy number changes, and repeat expansions can be central to understanding cancer and constitutional disorders. The relevant features may span hundreds of thousands or millions of base pairs. Their significance lies in the organization of the genome, not just the identity of individual nucleotides.

Consider a heterogeneous tumor. An oncologist needs to know more than whether the average cancer cell is likely to respond to treatment. A population of cells that won’t respond may be what matters most. There is enormous value in looking more deeply into that heterogeneity.

Short-read sequencing is well suited to detecting single-nucleotide variants and small indels at depth. Its economics matter because they determine how deeply we can look. But sequence depth is not the same thing as long-range structural information. Collecting more of one does not necessarily provide the other.

Measure structure efficiently

At Nabsys, we approach that problem through electronic genome mapping (EGM). The starting point is intact, ultra-long DNA, with molecules spanning hundreds of kilobases to megabases. We attach site-specific molecular tags and detect them electronically as the DNA passes through solid-state nanochannels. The positions of those tags provide a map of genomic structure. We can measure across large genomic features rather than reconstructing their structure from short fragments. We also retain the surrounding context needed to interpret those features.

EGM also measures individual molecules. The difference is what we ask the measurement to resolve. We are not trying to identify every nucleotide, but rather the arrangement of label patterns along a lengthy DNA molecule. That distinction has a large effect on speed. EGM measures DNA at roughly 1 million base pairs/second. Not having to read every base allows us to move much faster while retaining the long-range information needed to characterize structural variation.

The objective is not to replace sequencing. It is to obtain structural information without paying the cost of generating base-level information that the question does not require. Short-read sequencing and EGM can therefore address different parts of the same biological problem. In fact, these technologies complement each other to provide the highest resolution of the human genome from single base pair (with sequencing) to whole chromosome level changes (with EGM).

Build around the question

There are important qualifications. Single-molecule economics depends on detector design and density, not just the difficulty of detecting a molecule. Improvements in those areas can narrow cost differences. Short-read approaches are also extending their structural reach through proximity ligation, linked reads, and computational inference. The boundaries between methods are not fixed.

But improvement does not mean convergence. Technologies can become substantially better without becoming equally good, or equally economical, at every measurement.

I expect genomics to develop around complementary technologies, each matched to the information it can deliver most effectively. Short reads provide economic base-level depth. Long reads provide sequence across longer stretches of DNA. EGM provides long-range structural measurement without requiring every base to be sequenced.

As we learn more about how large-scale genomic alterations drive disease, demand for structural measurement will grow. Meeting that demand requires more than technical capability. A method also has to be affordable and practical, with a workflow that makes it usable at scale. Making structural measurement more accessible changes which studies can be done, and which questions can be answered.

The goal is not to put every genomic question on one platform. It is to make sure the cost of the measurement does not prevent us from asking the question.

 

Barrett Bready, MD, is the CEO of Nabsys and adjunct professor at Brown University. Contact: lulla@nabsys.com
